options: judicial review

items.explanation: The term “Bleeding Kansas” refers to the battle in Kansas between proslavery and abolitionist forces. The doctrine of popular sovereignty had created the circumstances that led to the gruesome conflict; it left the slave status of each territory up to its residents, to be decided at the time when the territory was ready to write a constitution and apply for statehood. Both sides wanted Kansas badly, and both sent representatives into the territory to form governments. President Pierce recognized the proslavery government, but abolitionist forces cried “foul” and continued their fight to establish Kansas as a free state. More than 200 people died in the resulting skirmishes.

items.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the excerpt above?
options: Lincoln won the populous Northern states; McClellan carried sparser ones.
Lincoln won the Election of 1864 because of Union successes during the Civil War.
The Emancipation Proclamation mobilized Black voters in the South to vote for Lincoln in the Election of 1864.
Republicans managed to gain control of Congress through the efforts of Lincoln to campaign on their behalf.
items.explanation: This question is all about Process of Elimination (POE). There is no mention of Black voters, so rule out (C). Choice (D) is tempting, but you don’t know for sure if Lincoln was campaigning for any other Republicans. Choice (B) is likewise unsupported. Choice (A) must be true because Lincoln won so many Electoral College votes. New Jersey and Delaware are relatively small states, while Kentucky was rural in 1864.
items.stimulus: Paraphrased excerpt (facts and statistics only; not a quotation) — “1864: Lincoln v. McClellan,” Harpweek.com: About 78 percent of the Union electorate cast ballots in 1864. Lincoln won reelection in an Electoral College landslide, 212 votes to McClellan’s 21, and took about 55 percent of the popular vote — the third-largest share of the nineteenth century. McClellan carried only New Jersey, Delaware, and Kentucky. Lincoln’s coalition drew heavily on native-born farmers, skilled and professional workers, voters of New England descent, younger voters, and military personnel (he won an estimated 78 percent of the Union soldier and sailor vote); Democrats ran strongest in the cities and among Irish- and German-American voters. Republicans also widened their congressional majorities (149 to 42 in the House, 42 to 10 in the Senate), retook several state legislatures, and lost only the New Jersey governorship.

items.stem: The dispute over electoral votes in the election of 1876
options: was similar to the election of 2000 in that the Supreme Court ultimately had to step in and decide the election
was resolved by a special bipartisan commission and resulted in the end of military reconstruction
led many members of Congress to push for a Constitutional amendment to abolish the Electoral College
was resolved when Samuel J. Tilden conceded the election to Rutherford
items.explanation: The election of 1876 is another of the disputed elections in American political history. Although Samuel J. Tilden, then governor of New York, won the popular vote nationwide, there were several states that contested the results of the election. Consequently, a special bipartisan commission was set up to determine the outcome of the election. In what became known as the “Compromise of 1877,” Rutherford B. Hayes won the presidential election by a margin of one single electoral vote. Hayes had promised to remove federal troops still stationed in the South after the Civil War, thus ending military reconstruction.

"We rely greatly on the sure operation of a complete blockade of the Atlantic and Gulf ports soon to commence. In connection with such a blockade we propose a powerful movement down the Mississippi to the Gulf... the effect would be to isolate the rebellious states and cut off their foreign trade."
—Gen. Winfield Scott, outlining the 'Anaconda Plan,' 1861 (abridged)
items.pd_rationale: Published 1861 (J. B. Elliott; entered per Act of Congress; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
items.suggested_stimulus: "Scott's Great Snake," J. B. Elliott, 1861 (Library of Congress). The map's depiction of the vast Southern coastline and territory supports the key (the Confederacy's sheer size).

items.explanation: Copperheads were Northern Democrats who denounced the war as ruinous and demanded peace — Lincoln's most bitter domestic foes.
options: A. Northern Democrats who opposed the war
B. Northern Republicans who wanted Lincoln replaced
C. Northern Democrats who rallied to Lincoln
D. Southern Democrats seeking early negotiations
